# Round 4 review

*Generated by the AI treasury analyst (claude-sonnet-5-5) on Oct 27, 2026.*

**Question:** Review Round 4.

**Position**

Karthik sold 60,000 units forward on a fixed-price swap at $85.0. The other 40,000 units floated. He held no collar, because collars did not exist until Round 5. His hedge ratio was 60.0%.

**Karthik's reasoning at the time**

This comes from the memo "Round 3 result + Round 4 decision" (Nov 3, 2025). He chose "Option B - Hedge 60% (60,000 units) at a fixed swap price of $85." He wrote that the aim was to "make sure the company is protected if prices fall a lot" and to avoid "the big $20M bankruptcy hit." He kept 40% unhedged so the firm could still "benefit if the market price ends up being higher than $85."

The memo refers to a "$5M minimum." The round data show a bankruptcy line of $4.00M. His logic held, but he was working from a threshold that was too high. His memo for Round 4's result (Nov 10, 2025) uses the correct $4M line.

**What happened**

Spot settled at $56.50. The swap paid $1.71M. Hedged revenue was $7.36M, and the recomputed figure matches his memo. Fully unhedged revenue would have been $5.65M, so the hedge added $1.71M.

Both outcomes were above the $4.00M bankruptcy line, so no penalty applied. Neither reached the $11.00M investment hurdle, so the project was not funded. An unhedged firm would have needed a spot price of $110.0 to clear the hurdle.

**Risk before the trade**

The stress test used 10,000 scenarios at 74.4% per-round volatility and a forward price of $85.0.

| Metric | Actual book (60% swap) | Unhedged |
|---|---|---|
| Expected revenue | $8.52M | $8.54M |
| 5th percentile revenue | $5.84M | $1.86M |
| VaR95 | $2.68M | $6.69M |
| ES95 | $2.86M | $7.14M |
| Worst case | $5.21M | $281K |
| Probability of bankruptcy | 0.0% | 25.8% |
| Probability of clearing hurdle | 13.2% | 24.0% |

The hedge cut VaR95 by 60.0% and removed the bankruptcy risk. It cost $26K of expected revenue. It also reduced the chance of clearing the hurdle by 10.8 percentage points, from 24.0% to 13.2%.

**Alternatives tested**

Bankruptcy probability was already 0.0%, so more protection was not needed. The cost was the lower chance of clearing the hurdle. I therefore tested smaller swaps. Only swap size was varied, because collars were not available in Round 4.

- **40,000-unit swap.** I chose it as a modest step down from 60,000. The hurdle probability rose to 18.2% (+5.0 points). Bankruptcy probability rose to 0.7%. VaR95 was $4.01M and ES95 was $4.28M. The 5th percentile revenue was $4.51M.
- **30,000-unit swap.** I chose it to see whether a larger cut in hedging bought much more upside. The hurdle probability was 20.1% (+6.9 points). Bankruptcy probability rose to 6.6%. VaR95 was $4.68M, and the 5th percentile revenue of $3.85M fell below the $4.00M line.
- **20,000-unit swap.** I chose it as the lightest hedge that still hedges part of the book. The hurdle probability was 21.6% (+8.4 points). Bankruptcy probability rose to 13.9%. VaR95 was $5.35M.

Expected revenue barely moved in any case, between $8.52M and $8.53M. The hurdle probability stayed below the unhedged 24.0% in every case. Each step toward it added bankruptcy risk, and a bankruptcy costs $20M.

**Verdict**

On the information available, the 60% swap was a sound decision. It removed a 25.8% chance of bankruptcy for a $26K reduction in expected revenue. Smaller swaps raised the hurdle probability by only 5.0 to 8.4 points. They also brought bankruptcy probabilities of 0.7% to 13.9%, against a $20M penalty. The $7.36M outcome came from the swap paying in a falling market. That is hindsight and is not what justifies the trade.

His reasoning was correct, but he cited the wrong threshold. The $5M figure in his memo was not the $4M line. Next time he should check the stated line before sizing the hedge.

The 40,000-unit swap was the only alternative close to his 60,000-unit choice. It raised the hurdle probability by 5.0 points but added 0.7% bankruptcy probability and raised VaR95 by 50%. I would not change the 60% hedge. If the firm values the project, the better route is a design that keeps upside above $85, such as a collar. That was not available in Round 4.
